content_groups.group_title: "What is the difference between low-lying placenta and placenta praevia?"

blocks.text: "Placenta praevia refers to placental tissue covering the internal cervical os, whereas a low-lying placenta is close to the internal os without covering it."

"This is a 32-week pregnant woman with recurrent painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. She is haemodynamically stable, and the uterus is soft and non-tender. Ultrasound demonstrates the placenta covering the internal cervical os, confirming placenta praevia. I would avoid digital vaginal examination, assess maternal and fetal wellbeing, check haemoglobin and blood group/Rh status, provide appropriate counselling and plan specialist follow-up and delivery."

"This woman with known placenta praevia is currently haemodynamically unstable with significant ongoing vaginal bleeding. I would treat this as a major obstetric haemorrhage, initiate ABC resuscitation, obtain large-bore IV access, activate the appropriate haemorrhage protocol, send urgent blood tests and arrange blood products. I would involve senior obstetric and anaesthetic teams and prepare for emergency delivery once maternal stabilisation is underway."

"This patient has a presentation highly suggestive of placenta praevia. I would first assess maternal haemodynamic stability and fetal wellbeing. If there is significant bleeding, I would initiate ABC resuscitation, obtain large-bore IV access, send FBC, group and crossmatch and coagulation studies including fibrinogen where appropriate, and activate the major obstetric haemorrhage protocol if required. I would perform an abdominal examination but avoid digital vaginal examination until the placental location has been established. I would use ultrasound, including transvaginal ultrasound when appropriate, to assess the relationship of the placenta to the internal cervical os. I would assess fetal wellbeing with CTG and ultrasound, correct maternal anaemia, consider anti-D in an eligible RhD-negative woman, and give antenatal corticosteroids if preterm delivery is anticipated. If placenta praevia persists near term, delivery is usually by planned Caesarean section, with timing based on the bleeding history and maternal and fetal circumstances. If previous Caesarean sections are present, I would specifically assess for placenta accreta spectrum and arrange multidisciplinary delivery planning."
